How Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed Helped Ignite a Challenge to Chuck Schumer
 
Plus, Mark Walter made Magic Johnson a billionaire—and test how much you know about wine with our quiz
 
 
TOM WILLIAMS/CQ ROLL CALL/ZUMA PRESS
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

Incoming Michigan Democratic Sen. Abdul El-Sayed is emerging as one of his party’s most disruptive forces after helping propel a challenge to Senate leadership that is gaining steam.

 

The 42-year-old epidemiologist was among the first to publicly call on Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen to run against New York Sen. Chuck Schumer for the party’s top leadership post. About half a dozen Democratic senators have backed Van Hollen’s long-shot bid ahead of the Dec. 1 vote.

 

El-Sayed’s pressure on Schumer suggests he will shift his party’s traditional alliances in ways that unsettle both sides of the aisle. His victory in Michigan has handed him a national stage to push sweeping changes to healthcare, campaign finance and U.S. foreign aid.

 

In an interview with Sabrina Siddiqui, El-Sayed was unsparing in his criticism of his own party while firing barbs at Republicans.

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

Basketball made Magic Johnson famous. Mark Walter made him a billionaire.

 

NBA superstar Earvin “Magic” Johnson made a killing in the years since retiring from the Los Angeles Lakers in 1996, investing in movie theaters, shopping centers and retail franchises that served predominantly Black and Latino communities. Yet it took a partnership with an unlikely teammate—Midwest insurance magnate Mark Walter—to make Johnson a billionaire, beginning with an invitation from Walter to invest in EquiTrust Life Insurance, a firm now linked to a federal probe. Looking back, Walter appears the prime beneficiary of the decadelong relationship, report Margot Patrick, Shane Shifflett and Justin Baer. While Johnson isn’t accused of any wrongdoing, his business dealings with Walter could draw scrutiny from investigators.

 

5.

 

Paying for mom and dad’s eldercare is ripping up some adult kids’ financial futures.

 

Soaring eldercare costs are remaking the finances of American families. Those with means are liquidating assets to pay for care. Adult children are abandoning careers, turning their homes into improvised care facilities and burning through significant sums, reports Jeanne Whalen. It’s a striking dynamic for the current generation of older Americans who have amassed record wealth and are living longer, more adventurous lives. But the onset of dementia or other diseases associated with aging can upend expectations for the sunset years. Many believe Medicare pays for long-term care, such as nursing homes and at-home caregivers, and are shocked to learn that it doesn’t.
